content_units: NSW Sole Trader to Pty Ltd: What Changes and Why

For a freelance graphic designer in New South Wales earning about   AUD 180,000   with   one owner  , moving to a   proprietary limited company (Pty Ltd)   usually means setting up a separate legal entity, shifting contracts/invoicing/tax registrations into that entity, and taking on   director compliance duties  .
Working context
- Business is currently operating as a   sole trader   in Australia.
- New structure will be a   single-shareholder, single-director Pty Ltd  .
- Revenue level means   GST registration should already apply   and will usually continue.
- This is a practical checklist, not legal or tax advice.
Registration and Setup Checklist
Phase   Goal   Key Tasks   Deliverable
1. Structure decision   Confirm Pty Ltd is worth it   Compare tax, asset protection, admin cost, payroll needs; choose company name; decide shareholder/director setup   Clear go/no-go decision

2. Company formation   Create the legal entity   Register company with ASIC; obtain ACN; choose constitution or replaceable rules; issue initial shares; set up company register   Registered Pty Ltd with ACN

3. Tax registrations   Put the company on the ATO system   Apply for ABN for the company; register TFN; register or maintain GST under company; consider PAYG withholding if paying salary; check payroll tax exposure if staff grow later   Company tax profile active

4. Banking and finance   Separate business money properly   Open company bank account; move software subscriptions and merchant facilities; update accounting file; set director loan rules if owner paid setup costs personally   Clean company bookkeeping

5. Commercial transition   Move trading activity to the company   Update invoices, quotes, website, email footer, business name holder, client contracts, IP clauses, privacy terms; notify clients of new entity   Clients contract with company

6. Insurance and risk   Protect the new entity   Review professional indemnity, public liability, cyber cover, equipment cover, workers compensation if required; update insured name to company   Policies in company name

7. Ongoing compliance   Avoid director and ATO problems   BAS and GST lodgments; company tax return; annual ASIC review; maintain records; super and STP if taking salary; minutes/resolutions   Ongoing compliance calendar
Practical Decision Checklist
1) Before registering the company
Option 1: Confirm why you are incorporating   Better asset separation, easier scaling, cleaner brand for agency-style work   Main trade-off: more admin and cost
ASIC company guide
Option 2: Check whether the business name can stay the same   You may keep the trading name, but ownership/registration usually needs updating to the company   Name availability matters
Check business name
Option 3: Decide how you will take money out   Usually salary, director fees, dividends, or some mix; each has different tax treatment   Get accountant input before first payment
ATO for companies
2) Core documents usually involved
-   ASIC company registration record
Includes company name, ACN, registered office, principal place of business, director, shareholder, and share structure.
-   Company constitution   or reliance on   replaceable rules
A custom constitution is often useful even for one-owner companies.
-   Initial share issue record
Usually one shareholder with ordinary shares.
-   Company register and minute book
Keep director/shareholder resolutions, share records, and key company decisions.
-   ABN, TFN, GST registration confirmations   for the company
These are separate from the sole trader registrations.
-   New client service agreement / updated terms of trade
The contracting party must be the company, not you personally.
-   IP assignment or confirmation document
Especially important if old designs, templates, logos, or brand assets need to be owned/licensed by the company.
-   Novation or assignment letters for existing contracts
Useful where current clients have ongoing retainers signed with the sole trader.
-   Updated invoice template
Should show company legal name, ABN, and GST treatment.
-   Employment/payroll records   if the company pays you wages
Includes STP setup, PAYG withholding, super arrangements.
-   Insurance certificates   in the company name
Existing sole trader policies may not automatically protect the company.
3) Tax and GST points to decide early
-   GST
At   AUD 180,000 revenue  , GST registration is generally required. The   company needs its own GST registration   even if the sole trader was already registered.
-   ABN/TFN
The company needs its   own ABN and TFN  . Your sole trader ABN does not transfer across.
-   Income tax
Company profits are taxed in the company, generally at the applicable company tax rate. Personal tax then depends on how money is paid to you.
-   Salary vs dividends
If you pay yourself a wage, the company may need   PAYG withholding  ,   Single Touch Payroll  , and   superannuation   compliance. Dividends require sufficient company profits and proper records.
-   Transferring business assets
If you move equipment, software rights, or goodwill into the company, ask your accountant about   CGT, depreciation, and small business concessions  .
-   BAS continuity
Plan the cutover date carefully so sales/expenses before and after incorporation are reported by the correct entity.
-   PSI/alienation of personal services income risk
For a solo creative business where income is mainly from your own labour and skill,   PSI rules may still matter   even if you use a company. This is a key accountant review point.
4) Insurance checklist
Option 1: Professional indemnity   Important for design errors, IP disputes, client loss claims   Often requested by corporate clients
Business insurance info
Option 2: Public liability   Useful if meeting clients on-site, at studios, events, or coworking spaces   Covers third-party injury/property damage risk
Insurance basics
Option 3: Cyber and equipment cover   Helpful for ransomware, data loss, laptops, cameras, tablets, and business interruption   Increasingly relevant for designers
Cyber security guide
5) Contract updates you should not skip
- Replace your current terms so the   company is the service provider  .
- Update   scope, revision limits, payment timing, late fees, and approval process  .
- Make   intellectual property ownership/licensing   explicit.
- Include   moral rights consents   where relevant.
- Add   portfolio use rights   so you can still display work unless clients require confidentiality.
- Review   indemnity, liability caps, and exclusion of consequential loss  .
- Update   privacy wording   if you collect client/customer data.
- For current clients, use a   novation or fresh contract   rather than just emailing “my business has changed”.
6) Director duties and ongoing company obligations
As sole director, you are legally responsible for the company’s compliance.
- Act with   care and diligence  .
- Act in   good faith   and for a proper purpose.
- Avoid improper use of your position or company information.
- Keep   financial records   and company registers.
- Ensure the company can   pay its debts when due  ; do not trade while insolvent.
- Lodge ASIC annual review items and keep details up to date.
- Meet ATO obligations:   BAS, company tax return, PAYG, super  , and recordkeeping where applicable.
For a one-owner company, the big practical difference is this:   the company’s money is not your personal money  . Treat drawings, reimbursements, wages, and dividends properly.
Common Failure Points for Small Creative Businesses
- Registering the company but continuing to sign contracts   personally  .
- Using the new company name on marketing, but leaving   banking, Stripe/PayPal, and invoicing   in the old sole trader setup.
- Forgetting to move or re-register   GST/ABN   to the company.
- Assuming incorporation automatically solves   PSI tax issues  .
- Mixing personal and company spending in one account.
- Paying yourself irregularly without classifying amounts as   salary, dividend, reimbursement, or director loan  .
- Keeping insurance in the sole trader name only.
- Failing to document transfer of   IP, equipment, software licenses, or client retainers  .
- Not checking whether clients require the new company to provide updated   W-8/W-9 style vendor forms, insurance certificates, or procurement onboarding  .
- Ignoring ASIC annual review fees and deadlines.
